summary: Space Adventures is a browser-based educational game that lets players plan and carry out a robotic space mission, inspired by real NASA, ESA and JAXA missions. Players start on Earth, build and prepare their mission, fly a spacecraft to a real destination, explore it to collect samples and make discoveries, and transmit their findings home. Energy and storage are limited, so every choice affects the next stage. It addresses the challenge by turning real mission science into something people can play.
details:
Space Adventures is a browser-based educational game that takes players through a robotic space mission: Earth → Build → Fly → Explore → Transmit. Players choose a real destination, such as 101955 Bennu from NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission (2016–2023), and prepare their mission. They then pilot a spacecraft in the Outbound flight stage, using a flight deck that shows velocity, propellant, range, altitude and a proximity radar. After a safe touchdown they hand over to the research stage, where they collect samples and make discoveries. Limited energy and storage mean each choice affects later stages.

Benefits and intended impact
Most people never see the decisions, patience and trade-offs behind a space mission. The game lets students, teachers and curious players experience them hands-on, and it needs no installation. It runs in any modern browser and is published on GitHub Pages. We want players to leave with a better understanding of how real missions work.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules), with separate modules for physics, scene, HUD and mission logic. We used VS Code, Git and GitHub, with a branch for each stage, and GitHub Pages for publishing. No special hardware was needed. We built most of the code with AI coding assistants, and we directed the design, tested the results and integrated the stages.

Creativity
The game turns real mission data into a playable story, with a mission-control style interface. Each teammate built one stage that plugs into a shared integration contract, so the stages work together as one game.

Factors we considered
Scientific accuracy came first: we cite sources and separate observation from inference. Organic molecules are never presented as proof of life. We also considered accessibility (browser only, nothing to install), clear controls for new players, and keeping the code modular so teammates could work in parallel.
